nameStory: The blackberry lily gets its intriguing name from its distinctive seed pods that split open in fall to reveal clusters of shiny black seeds that look remarkably like blackberries! This clever mimicry helps the plant attract birds who mistake the seeds for actual berries and help disperse them. It's also called leopard lily because of the spotted orange petals that resemble a leopard's coat.
description: Blackberry lily is an ornamental perennial that looks more like a day lily than a traditional iris, despite being in the iris family. It grows 2-4 feet tall with sword-like leaves arranged in a fan pattern typical of irises. The showy orange flowers bloom in summer, each lasting just one day, followed by the plant's signature feature: distinctive seed pods that split open to reveal clusters of glossy black seeds that look exactly like blackberries.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature: seed pods split into three sections revealing clusters of shiny, jet-black seeds that look exactly like blackberries and rattle softly when shaken

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Six-petaled orange flowers heavily spotted with dark red or maroon dots, about 2 inches across, blooming in clusters at the top of branched stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Flat, sword-shaped leaves arranged in a fan pattern like other irises, feeling smooth and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in clumps 2-4 feet tall with multiple branching flower stems rising above the foliage, spreading slowly by underground rhizomes

habitat: Found in gardens, old homesites, and naturalized areas where it has escaped cultivation. Prefers well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade and is quite drought tolerant once established. Most commonly encountered as a garden escapee near abandoned properties or in areas where garden waste has been dumped.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as typical iris-like fans of green leaves. No flowers yet, but the distinctive leaf arrangement helps identify it among other emerging perennials.
seasonality.summer: Peak bloom time with eye-catching orange, spotted flowers opening daily. Each flower lasts just one day, but new ones keep opening in succession for weeks.
seasonality.fall: The magic happens as seed pods ripen and split open to reveal those remarkable blackberry-like seed clusters. The seeds persist well into fall, rattling in their pods.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, leaving only the dried seed stalks with empty pods if they haven't been harvested by birds or fallen off.

funFact: This plant is such a master of disguise that it was originally classified in its own genus (Belamcanda) for over 200 years until DNA testing in 2005 revealed it was actually an iris in disguise - it had fooled botanists just as well as it fools birds with its fake blackberries!
confusionNotes: The orange, spotted flowers might be confused with tiger lilies, but blackberry lily flowers have six equal petals in a flat, symmetrical pattern while tiger lilies have curved-back petals. The distinctive iris-like leaves and those unmistakable blackberry seed clusters make identification certain.
contextualKnowledge: This plant causes naming confusion because it's neither a blackberry nor a traditional lily - it's actually an iris! Originally from Asia, it was widely planted in colonial gardens and has been naturalizing ever since. The scientific name changed relatively recently when DNA studies reshuffled the iris family tree.
compareHints: Unlike other New England irises that have blue, purple, or yellow flowers, blackberry lily is the only one with orange, spotted blooms. While most irises have typical iris-shaped flowers with falls and standards, blackberry lily has flat, six-petaled flowers more like a lily. The seed pods are also unique - other irises produce dry capsules, not these berry-like clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern blue flag is much larger and more robust than slender blue flag, which has narrow, grass-like leaves and smaller flowers.
Yellow iris is the only consistently yellow-flowered iris you'll find growing wild in New England wetlands - all our native iris species like northern blue flag have blue or purple flowers.
Japanese Iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by its gray-green (rather than bright green) leaves and reddish-purple flower tones instead of pure blue-purple.
Slender blue flag is much more delicate than the common northern blue flag, with leaves that are dramatically narrower (pencil-width vs.

Unlike its freshwater-loving cousins like northern blue flag (which grows in marshes and pond edges), beach-head iris is the only New England iris that can survive in pure beach sand with constant salt exposure.
Dwarf crested iris is dramatically smaller than all other New England irises - while northern blue flag and yellow iris tower at 2-4 feet tall in wetlands, this woodland species stays under 6 inches.
Unlike New England's native blue flag irises which are tall wetland plants, netted iris is tiny and prefers dry, well-drained soils.
Compared to northern blue flag, southern blue flag typically has broader, more rounded flower petals and slightly wider leaves.
Sweet iris differs from New England's native blue flag irises by its sweet fragrance and slightly more purple-tinted flowers.
Siberian iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by having much narrower, more grass-like leaves and more compact growth, while Yellow Iris has broader leaves and bright yellow flowers.
Japanese iris differs from native blue flags by its massive, completely flat flowers and preference for consistently wet, acidic soil.
Unlike our common northern blue flag with its blue-purple flowers or the invasive yellow iris with bright yellow blooms, cemetery iris stands out with pure white flowers.
